When traders start looking for a charting and analysis platform, the **[TradingView](https://in.tradingview.com/?aff_id=167054) vs Thinkorswim comparison** often tops the list. Both tools are popular, but they serve slightly different audiences and come with distinct strengths. In this guide we’ll break down the core aspects of each platform so you can decide which one fits your style, budget, and trading goals.

## Overview
Thinkorswim, owned by TD Ameritrade (now part of Charles Schwab), is a desktop‑centric suite that integrates brokerage services with advanced analytics. TradingView, on the other hand, began as a web‑based charting community and has grown into a multi‑device platform that also offers brokerage integration through select partners. If you already have a Schwab account, Thinkorswim feels like a natural extension; if you prefer a browser‑first experience with social sharing, TradingView may be more appealing.

## Key Features
Both platforms pack a punch, but they emphasize different areas.

### Charting Tools
Thinkorswim offers over 400 technical studies, drawing tools, and customizable layouts directly within the desktop app. Its thinkScript language lets you build custom indicators and alerts with a fair amount of power. TradingView shines with its Pine Script editor, which is arguably easier for beginners, and its cloud‑based charts update instantly across devices. The community library on TradingView also provides thousands of public scripts you can import with a click.

### Order Execution
Thinkorswim provides direct market access for stocks, options, futures, and forex, letting you place trades from the same window where you analyze charts. TradingView does not execute trades natively; instead, it routes orders through partnered brokers (e.g., Forex.com, OANDA, or Interactive Brokers). This separation means you’ll need to maintain a broker account elsewhere, but it also keeps the charting side lightweight.

### Paper Trading
Both platforms offer simulated trading. Thinkorswim’s paperMoney feature mirrors live account balances and lets you test strategies in real‑time market conditions. TradingView’s paper trading is integrated into its chart interface, allowing you to place mock trades directly on the chart and review performance via a simple journal.

### Mobile App
Thinkorswim’s mobile app mirrors much of the desktop functionality, though some advanced studies are limited due to screen size. TradingView’s mobile experience is highly praised for its responsiveness; the same charts and scripts you build on desktop appear almost identically on phone or tablet, making it ideal for traders who are constantly on the go.

## Pricing Plans
Cost can be a deciding factor, especially for beginners.

### Thinkorswim Pricing
Thinkorswim is free to use if you have a funded TD Ameritrade/Charles Schwab account. There are no subscription fees for the platform itself; you only pay standard trading commissions (which are $0 for stocks and ETFs, $0.65 per options contract, etc.). If you don’t have a brokerage account, you’ll need to open one to access the software.

### TradingView Pricing
TradingView operates on a freemium model. The free tier gives you basic charts with limited indicators and one saved layout. Paid plans start at $14.95/month (Pro), $29.95/month (Pro+), and $49.95/month (Premium). Higher tiers unlock more indicators per chart, multiple layouts, priority customer support, and extended historical data. Many traders find the Pro+ plan sufficient for serious analysis.

## Community & Support
The social aspect can enhance learning and idea generation.

### Thinkorswim Community
Thinkorswim’s community is largely broker‑driven. You’ll find webinars, tutorials, and a user forum hosted by Schwab. The thinkScript community is active, but the platform lacks a built‑in social feed where users share chart ideas in real time.

### TradingView Community
TradingView excels here. Users can publish trading ideas, comment on others’ charts, and follow traders they admire. The platform’s social network feels like a mix of Twitter and a charting forum, making it easy to discover new strategies or get feedback on your own setups. Additionally, TradingView offers an extensive help center, video tutorials, and a responsive ticket system for paid users.

## Which Platform Fits You?
Choosing between Thinkorswim and TradingView boils down to your workflow and priorities.

- **Stick with Thinkorswim** if you already have a Schwab account, prefer an all‑in‑one
